justice: There is a continuous paved pedestrian edge on the left side with a raised curb separating the planting strip from the roadway, indicating some dedicated pedestrian space allocation.

On-street/edge parking occupies much of the right-side margin of the roadway (e.g., the red car in the foreground), reducing shared space for non-motorized users and weakening equitable distribution among modes.
No visible curb ramps, tactile paving, or marked crossing points are present in the scene, limiting barrier-free accessibility and reducing consistent usability across different user needs.
safety: The street is narrow and carries mixed traffic (a scooter/motorbike is traveling in-lane), with no visible protected separation for cyclists or pedestrians, increasing potential conflicts.
Parked cars line the right side and appear close to the travel lane, creating dooring risk and reducing sightlines for both drivers and riders.

Lane edge markings (yellow line) provide some guidance, but there are no visible speed-calming elements (speed humps/raised crossings) or clear pedestrian priority features, lowering overall perceived safety.
livability: The left side has a landscaped green strip with shrubs and trees adjacent to housing, which supports a more pleasant daily environment.

The setting appears primarily residential (apartment block on the left, low-rise buildings/wall on the right) with limited visible active frontage or street-level amenities, which may reduce street vitality.
Few people are visible and there are no evident benches, small plazas, or social nodes; this limits opportunities for lingering and neighborhood interaction.
sustainability: Substantial tree and shrub planting on the left provides ecological benefits (shade potential, habitat, and air-quality support).
A scooter/motorbike is present and the street appears suitable for short local trips, which can support lower-carbon mobility compared with longer car trips.

However, car dominance is still evident (multiple parked vehicles), and there is no visible public-transport stop, bike parking, or cycling facility that would further encourage sustainable mode shift.
aesthetics: Greenery along the left side improves visual softness and provides a more pleasant streetscape edge compared with fully hardscaped corridors.
The right side is dominated by a long blank wall and utilitarian building facades, creating a monotonous visual experience and weaker street character.
The presence of multiple parked cars in the foreground and along the street adds visual clutter and reduces the perceived neatness of the corridor.
comfort: Tree canopy on the left provides partial shade and improves thermal comfort for users near that side of the street.
The roadway surface appears smooth and well-maintained, supporting physical comfort for driving and riding (and for walking if pedestrians must share the carriageway).
There are no visible benches or resting features, and the pedestrian realm is narrow/unclear on the right (dominated by wall and parked cars), which can reduce psychological comfort for walking.
walkability: A defined curb and landscaped buffer on the left can improve walking experience by separating pedestrians from moving vehicles.
Sidewalk continuity and width are not clearly legible throughout the scene, and the right side offers little pedestrian refuge due to the wall and parked vehicles.
There are no visible crosswalks, curb ramps, or pedestrian signage, which reduces pedestrian priority and makes walking less convenient and legible.
bikeability: No dedicated bike lane markings or protected cycling infrastructure are visible; cyclists would need to mix with motor vehicles in a narrow lane.
Parked cars along the travel edge create dooring and pinch-point risks for cyclists, especially near the red car in the foreground.
There is no visible bicycle parking, wayfinding, or intersection/crossing treatments that would improve cycling convenience and perceived safety.
